title: The conclave
hook: cardinals under eighty lock themselves in the Sistine Chapel and vote until white smoke

segments.voice: Yesterday, Easter Monday: a pope died while the Church was still singing Easter. Your line was the day after easter.

The doors of the Sistine Chapel are about to close, and a voice calls out two Latin words: extra omnes. Everyone out. Staff, cameras, guards: out. Inside, under the painted ceiling, sit the cardinals who are allowed to vote. Their phones are gone. No news, no messages in or out. They will stay inside this closed world, praying and voting, until one name has enough votes to make a pope. Outside, a crowd in Saint Peter's Square stares at a thin metal chimney on the chapel roof, waiting for smoke.
screen: `EXTRA OMNES: EVERYONE OUT.` → `NO PHONES, NO NEWS.` → `A CROWD WATCHES A CHIMNEY.`

segments.voice: Conclave names both the gathering and the locked-in way it works. Today's rules come from a document John Paul the Second wrote on electing a pope, later adjusted by Benedict. Only cardinals under eighty may vote, and they swear to keep everything secret. The ballot is a card printed with the Latin for I elect as Supreme Pontiff, and a blank line. Each cardinal writes one name, in handwriting meant to be hard to recognize. One at a time, he carries his folded card to the altar, beneath the great painting of the Last Judgment, and says an oath aloud: he calls Christ the Lord, who will be his judge, to witness that he is voting for the one he believes, before God, should be chosen. It takes two-thirds of the votes to elect. After the counting, the ballots are burned in a stove. Black smoke means no one yet. White smoke, with the bells of Saint Peter's, means a pope, and a cardinal steps onto the balcony to announce: habemus papam, we have a pope. The Church sees something old in this. In the Acts of the Apostles, before choosing someone to take the place of Judas, the apostles pray to the Lord who knows every heart and ask him to show whom he has chosen. Then they cast lots. The conclave keeps the prayer and trades the lots for ballots: human votes, counted carefully, held inside prayer. And this week's popes, the one who stepped down and the one from Buenos Aires, each walked out of this room.
screen: `UNDER EIGHTY, SWORN, AND LOCKED IN.` · `ONE NAME, IN DISGUISED HANDWRITING.` · `AN OATH AT THE ALTAR, CHRIST AS WITNESS.` · `BLACK SMOKE, THEN WHITE.` · then, large: `HABEMUS PAPAM.`

segments.voice: Take one choice in front of you into a closed room: no phone, no polls. Hold up each option, one at a time, the way a cardinal carries his card to the altar, and notice which one you could carry with a clear conscience. If you pray, ask, as the apostles did, to be shown the way; you don't have to decide yet, and black smoke is allowed.
Conclave. The locked gathering of cardinals that elects a pope, voting in the Sistine Chapel until one name has two-thirds of the votes.
Your line: white smoke. A decision, made and announced. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: When the papacy is vacant, Catholics around the world pray at Mass for the cardinals in conclave, and crowds gather in Saint Peter's Square to watch the chimney for white smoke.

fork.setup: you're a cardinal in the Sistine Chapel, folded card in hand, walking to the altar. what do you do?
options: drop it in without a word.
say an oath, calling Christ as witness that you vote for the one God would choose.
read the name aloud so everyone knows.
fork.reveal: each cardinal says the oath aloud before casting his ballot. the name itself stays secret.

original.note: Latin: we have a pope, the words announced from the balcony after the white smoke.

trapdoor: what you thought: conclave is just a fancy word for a meeting.
what it means: the locked gathering of the cardinals who elect a pope, voting until white smoke.
what a scholar hears: the rite echoes Acts 1, where the apostles pray and then cast lots for Judas's replacement; the conclave keeps the prayer and uses ballots.

chat.says: How do they actually pick a new pope? Is it like an election campaign?
options: Cardinals under eighty, locked in, vote in secret under oath; it takes two-thirds.
All the world's bishops gather in Rome and vote, and a simple majority wins.
Every cardinal votes, whatever his age, and the one with the most votes wins.
chat.meaning: Only cardinals under eighty vote, sworn to secrecy, each carrying his ballot to the altar with an oath; two-thirds of the votes elect.

Sistine Chapel.meaning: the Vatican chapel where the cardinals vote

Last Judgment.meaning: the great painting above the chapel's altar

sources.ref: Universi Dominici Gregis (on the vacancy of the Apostolic See and the election of the Roman Pontiff), as amended by Benedict XVI
sources.work: Apostolic constitution of John Paul II

notes: Week-end day (932–938): the teach ends with a short look back at the week's stories.

Claims from Universi Dominici Gregis: electors under eighty; oath of secrecy; ballot reading 'Eligo in Summum Pontificem'; disguised handwriting; oath at the altar (paraphrased); two-thirds majority (restored by Benedict XVI); ballots burned. Confirm each.
Confirm 'extra omnes' is announced by the Master of Papal Liturgical Celebrations, and that bells accompany white smoke.
Etymology of 'conclave' (cum clave) hedged as 'usually explained'; confirm.
Acts 1:24 paraphrased, not quoted (Douay-Rheims wording not verified).
The cardinals' lodging and phones-surrendered detail kept general; confirm.

Editor: cut the 'cum clave' etymology from the teach and trapdoor (claims rule: no etymology the cited texts don't state); hook now says 'until one name has enough votes' (the elected need not be one of the electors); 'Catholics see' changed to 'The Church sees'.

Audit: Acts 1 chose Matthias by lots, not votes; the teach and trapdoor now say so instead of implying the apostles voted. 'After each count the ballots are burned' now 'after the counting' (UDG burns ballots after two scrutinies in a session when no one is elected).
